% =========================================================================
% Abstract — LCFM camera-ready: findings F1-F3, systems F4-F5 (kit section 3a)
% =========================================================================
% TODO AMAN: the title still frames the reviewed version's conclusion ("stops paying
% off"). The camera-ready's result is that speculation DOES still pay once the ring's
% rotation is removed, and that the decode stall was the rotation rather than
% speculation. I have kept the title because changing it is a decision for you, not a
% correction: alternatives are (a) "<...> The Ring's Rotation Was the Decode Step"
% or (b) "Stretching RoPE Costs a Quarter of Speculative Acceptance". Say which you
% want and I will retitle and recompile.
\begin{abstract}
Speculative decoding's short-context speedups do not survive
million-token inference, and the mechanism is not what the
technique's own literature would predict. We report three
scientific findings and one systems measurement, all on
8$\times$A100 80\,GB SXM4 in FP4 weights with an NF4 KV cache.
\emph{First}, on \texttt{meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B} --- a model that
ships the rotary-scaling dictionary the intervention modifies ---
stretching the rotary basis at 128\,k moves paired perplexity by
$+0.05\%$ (factor 16) and $+1.56\%$ (factor 32) while speculative
acceptance falls from $0.7272$ to $0.5336$/$0.5006$, a 27--31\%
relative loss. An intervention that is nearly free in likelihood
is expensive in acceptance, so acceptance is not a proxy for
perplexity and must be measured. \emph{Second}, greedy decoding at
long context degenerates into repetition --- 9 of 15 long-context
rows loop against 0 of 26 sampled rows at $T{=}0.7$ --- and a
looping row is trivially accepted by a greedy draft, so a greedy
acceptance number measures the degeneracy rather than the draft's
agreement with the target. \emph{Third}, the native-1M target stays
coherent at 1\,M: within $9.5\%$ of its own 128\,k perplexity on
the exactly aligned book.
\emph{Fourth}, in the systems section we localise the decode
bottleneck of the ring-attention engine we built: rotating each
layer's key/value shard around 8 ranks costs 256 rounds per decode
token, and a bare-process benchmark of the ring primitive shows
each round costs a fixed $\sim$10.3\,ms \emph{regardless of
payload} (4\,KB and 266\,MB are within 0.4\% of each other). The
decode step was therefore latency per round, not bandwidth.
Removing the rotation with split-KV --- prior work, Meta's pass-Q/pass-KV
and vLLM's Decode Context Parallelism --- is worth $2.8$--$5.3\times$
in decode time per token, and speculative decoding still pays
$2.0$--$2.3\times$ on top of it. The measurement also withdraws the
reviewed version's two systems claims, that ring communication was
${\leq}1.2\%$ of wall time and that the speedup regressed at
512\,k/1\,M.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{speculative decoding, ring attention, long-context LLM
inference, KV cache quantization, RoPE scaling, decode-side context
parallelism, distributed inference}

% =========================================================================
% Section 1 — Introduction
% =========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Long-context language model inference has emerged as the
rate-limiting step for several practical workloads: multi-document
question answering over book-length corpora, agentic workflows that
accumulate hours of tool-call traces, retrieval-free in-context
learning at the scale of a small library, and analysis of complete
code repositories.  Frontier closed-source systems already advertise
context windows in the millions of tokens.  Reproducing that
capability on commodity, open hardware --- 8 GPUs on a single node,
the configuration available to most academic and small-industry
groups --- requires solving two compounding bottlenecks
simultaneously.

\paragraph{Bottleneck 1 (memory).}
The key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length.  For
Llama-2-7B in bf16, a 1 million-token KV cache occupies approximately
512\,GiB --- far exceeding the 80\,GiB capacity of a single A100 ---
and the attention matrix for prefill scales quadratically.  Ring Attention
\citep{liu2023ringattention} resolves this by sharding the sequence
dimension across $W$ ranks and pipelining the per-block attention
computation through a ring of inter-rank exchanges.  Combined with
FlashAttention-2 \citep{dao2023flashattention2} for the local
attention kernel and KV quantization (NF4
\citep{dettmers2023qlora}, KIVI \citep{liu2024kivi},
KVQuant \citep{hooper2024kvquant}) for cache compression, sub-100\,GiB
per-rank footprints become feasible at 1\,M context.

\paragraph{Bottleneck 2 (latency).}
Once memory fits, autoregressive decoding remains expensive: each
generated token requires a full forward pass through the model, with
attention costs that grow with the context length already in the
KV cache.  Speculative decoding
\citep{leviathan2023fast,chen2023accelerating,miao2023specinfer,cai2024medusa}
amortizes this cost by having a small draft model propose $k$
tokens, then verifying all $k$ with a single target-model forward
pass and accepting the longest matching prefix.  When the draft and
target agree often (high \emph{acceptance rate} $\alpha$), the
target pays one forward to generate $1 + k\alpha$ tokens.  At
short context, this routinely yields $2\text{--}4\times$ speedups.

\paragraph{The question this paper asks.}
At short context, speculative decoding yields 2--3$\times$
speedups on standard inference benchmarks. We ask whether this
speedup transfers to million-token inference. Answering the
question requires a system that can run a target-model forward at
1\,M context on commodity hardware. Both ring attention and
speculative decoding exist as mature open-source components, but
they have not been combined into a published million-token
inference system. Doing so surfaces practical questions: how does
NF4 KV quantization interact with the YaRN \citep{peng2023yarn}
position scaling required to push Llama-2-7B past its 4\,k
training horizon; how does the speculative verify loop's
broadcast-and-resample pattern compose with the ring attention's
existing collective; and most importantly, \emph{does the
speculative speedup that exists at 4\,k transfer to 1\,M, or do
acceptance rates collapse out of the regime where the technique
is useful?}

\paragraph{The RASD system.}
We present \textbf{RASD} (Ring Attention with Speculative Decoding),
an inference system that combines (i) ring-attention sequence
parallelism, (ii) NF4 KV-cache quantization with chunked updates and
a bf16 outlier-keep prefix \citep{xiao2024streamingllm} on rank 0,
(iii) rotary (YaRN) position scaling where the target's training
horizon requires it, and (iv) speculative verification with a
1.3\,B-parameter draft model into a single end-to-end loop.  On
8$\times$A100 80\,GB SXM4, RASD runs a 1\,M-native Llama-3-8B target
at 1\,M context with \textbf{41.2\,GiB peak allocated per rank}
(69\,GiB reserved; the reviewed version's ``40\,GiB, half of 80'' was
a rank-0-only reading).  In the same hardware configuration, vanilla
HuggingFace FlashAttention-2 \texttt{generate()} runs out of memory
at 128\,k single-rank --- so a direct \emph{throughput} comparison at
long context is meaningless; the correct comparison is with an
apples-to-apples \emph{target-only} ablation that uses the same ring
infrastructure but disables the speculative loop.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E18); results/mlsys/CLAIMS.md C6

\paragraph{Empirical findings.}
We report the findings up-front. Three are scientific, two are
systems.
\emph{(F1) Stretching the rotary basis barely moves perplexity and
costs a quarter of speculative acceptance.} On
\texttt{meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B}, which ships the \texttt{rope\_scaling}
dictionary the intervention modifies, the paired perplexity ratio at
128\,k is $1.0005$ (factor 16) and $1.0156$ (factor 32) against
native, while acceptance falls from $0.7272$ to $0.5336$/$0.5006$
($-27\%$/$-31\%$), on all five books individually. An intervention
that is free in likelihood is expensive in acceptance.
% SRC: results/mlsys/sampling_session/session_a_rope_fix_gate.csv; ROPE_SAMP_{NATIVE,F16,F32}_SPEC
\emph{(F2) Greedy decoding loops at long context and inflates
acceptance.} Under greedy, 9 of 15 long-context rows degenerate into
repetition; under $T{=}0.7$ sampling, 0 of 26 rows do. A greedy draft
accepts a loop trivially, so a greedy acceptance number measures the
degeneracy, not the draft-target agreement --- which is why the
campaign that produced the reviewed version's acceptance numbers was
re-run under sampling.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 1 (census); results/mlsys/sampling_session/repetition_*.csv
\emph{(F3) The native-1M target is coherent at 1\,M.} Its own
perplexity at 1\,M is $1.805$ against $1.649$ at 128\,k on the
exactly aligned book, $+9.5\%$; on the two books that share
91--95\% of their scored tokens the difference is within $1.1\%$.
% SRC: results/mlsys/sampling_session/QUALITY_FIX_{128K,1M}; alignment.csv
\emph{(F4) Our own ring's key/value rotation was the decode step.}
Rotating each layer's K/V shard around the 8 ranks costs 8 rotations
$\times$ 32 layers $=$ \textbf{256 rounds per decode token}, and a
bare-process benchmark of the same primitive shows each round costs a
fixed $\approx$10.3\,ms \emph{whatever the payload}: 10.3124\,ms for
4\,KB and 10.3462\,ms for 266\,MB, a 66\,000$\times$ range with 0.4\%
variation. The decode step was latency per round, not bandwidth.
Removing the rotation (split-KV; prior work) is worth
$2.8$--$5.3\times$ in decode time per token, rising with context.
% SRC: results/mlsys/decode_df/ring_bench/ringbench.csv; RESULTS_OCT.md 10.2b
\emph{(F5) Speculation still pays on top of the fix}: $2.01\times$ /
$2.29\times$ / $2.20\times$ decode-only at 128\,k / 512\,k / 1\,M
over the same engine's target-only path ($1.95\times$ / $1.76\times$ /
$1.41\times$ end-to-end --- the 1\,M end-to-end figure is smaller
because 1\,M prefill is now the long pole), on three, three and five
books per arm.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md sections 10.2 and 10.7

Two claims from the reviewed version are \textbf{withdrawn} and are
not reported again: that ring communication was $\leq 1.2\%$ of wall
time (the profiler bucket recorded 0.31--0.37$\times$ of the physical
wire floor, so it did not capture the transfers), and that the
speedup regressed to $0.94\times$/$0.97\times$ at 512\,k/1\,M (not
reproduced by the paper's own same-code re-run; the decode path was
the mechanism, see F4).
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E1, E14)

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
  \item \textbf{A measured dissociation between perplexity and
        speculative acceptance} under rotary-basis stretching
        (F1): $-27$ to $-31\%$ acceptance for $+0.05$ to $+1.56\%$
        perplexity, on a model that ships the dictionary the
        intervention edits, with the direction holding on five of
        five books.
  \item \textbf{Evidence that greedy acceptance numbers at long
        context are measured on degenerate text} (F2), with the
        census, the detection rule, and the consequence: the
        headline matrix is sampled at $T{=}0.7$ and every row is
        checked for periodicity rather than assumed clean.
  \item \textbf{A coherence check of a native-1M target at 1\,M}
        (F3), with the alignment of the two rungs verified from the
        token records rather than from the pool's name.
  \item \textbf{A decode diagnosis and its confirmation} (F4): the
        ring's per-token K/V rotation is 256 rounds of a fixed-cost
        collective, so the ring was paying latency per round
        independently of context; removing the rotation with
        split-KV is $2.8$--$5.3\times$ decode-only, and the
        measurement is a bare-process benchmark of the primitive,
        not an inference from end-to-end timing.
  \item \textbf{A 1\,M-token inference capability} on 8$\times$A100
        80\,GB at 41.2\,GiB peak allocated per rank, with the
        chunked-NF4 + attention-sink cache design that fits it, and
        the per-rank memory equation.
  \item \textbf{A reference implementation} released under MIT with
        version-pinned dependencies, every per-position acceptance
        trace, every saved generation, per-rank memory snapshots,
        profiler JSONs, and the ablation grid that derived the
        design point.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{What this paper does not claim.} Split-KV is prior work
(Meta's pass-Q/pass-KV ring-context parallelism, vLLM's Decode
Context Parallelism); we cite it for the technique and claim only the
diagnosis and the measurement. The comparison against vLLM is
\textbf{not precision-matched}: vLLM is bf16 with bf16 KV and greedy
decoding, RASD is FP4 weights with an NF4 KV cache and $T{=}0.7$
sampling with speculation.

% =========================================================================
% Section 2 — Background / Related Work
% =========================================================================
\section{Background and Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

We synthesize three research threads --- long-context attention,
distributed LLM inference, and speculative decoding --- and identify
their structural intersection as the RASD design point.

\subsection{Attention efficiency and the long-context wall}
\label{sec:related-attention}

The transformer architecture \citep{vaswani2017attention} established
multi-head self-attention as the dominant sequence modelling
primitive. Its $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ memory cost in sequence length $N$
imposed a hard ceiling on context at the scale of a single
accelerator. Two orthogonal strategies have emerged.

\paragraph{Sparse and recurrent approximations.}
Longformer \citep{beltagy2020longformer} replaced full attention with a
sliding window of width $w$, reducing complexity to
$\mathcal{O}(N \cdot w)$ while adding global tokens to preserve
long-range reasoning. Transformer-XL \citep{dai2019transformerxl}
introduced segment-level recurrence. Both sacrifice expressiveness:
the window can lose critical context, and recurrence cannot revise
earlier representations in light of later tokens.

\paragraph{Exact IO-aware tiling.}
FlashAttention \citep{dao2022flashattention} demonstrated that the
$\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ memory barrier is separable from the
$\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute barrier. By tiling $Q, K, V$ into SRAM
blocks and fusing the kernel, FlashAttention keeps peak HBM at
$\mathcal{O}(N)$ while computing exact attention --- 2--4$\times$
faster than standard PyTorch attention. FlashAttention-2
\citep{dao2023flashattention2} refined the work partitioning.
This result is foundational: memory and compute need not scale
together. RASD uses FlashAttention-2 as the local-block kernel inside
its ring-attention layer.

The $\mathcal{O}(N)$ footprint still grows without bound. For
$N \sim 10^6$, even $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory at the per-layer level
($\sim$1\,MiB/token for a 13B model in bf16) exceeds single-device
capacity. \emph{A fundamentally multi-device approach is required.}

\paragraph{Architectural alternatives to attention.}
A separate line of work replaces attention with sub-quadratic
primitives. StripedHyena \citep{poli2023stripedhyena} interleaves
state-space convolution layers with attention layers, achieving
sub-quadratic compute at long context without the IO constraints
of attention. This direction is out of scope here because RASD is
architecture-agnostic: it runs the standard transformer and asks
how far inference engineering alone can push context length on
commodity hardware.

\subsection{Distributed inference}
\label{sec:related-distributed}

\paragraph{Ring Attention.}
\citet{liu2023ringattention} resolve the single-device memory barrier
by distributing the sequence dimension across $D$ devices in a
logical ring. Each device holds $s/D$ query, key, and value tokens.
KV blocks rotate clockwise one step per iteration; after $D-1$
rotations every query has attended to every KV block. The online
softmax recurrence of \citet{dao2022flashattention} ensures this is
numerically exact --- not an approximation. Communication and
compute are overlapped: while device $i$ attends to its current
block, it simultaneously sends that block to device $i-1$ and
receives the next from device $i+1$.

Per-device peak memory is $6bch$ --- where $b$ is batch size, $c$ is
block size, and $h$ is hidden dimension --- \emph{independent of
sequence length $s$}. Sequences exceeding one million tokens become
tractable on standard 8-GPU nodes. However, Ring Attention's original
evaluation focused on the \textbf{prefill phase} (processing an input
prompt); its \emph{decode-phase} behavior --- generating one new
token at a time over a massive distributed KV cache --- received
little treatment.

\paragraph{Decode-side context parallelism (prior work).}
That decode-phase gap is closed in the literature, and this paper
cites that work rather than claiming it. Meta's context-parallel
report \citep{meta2024contextparallelism} describes ring-context
parallelism for million-token inference in the pass-KV and pass-Q
forms: rather than rotating every key/value block around the ring for
each new query, a rank attends to the key/value blocks it already
holds and the partial results are combined, with the query replicated
(pass-Q) or the key/value replicated instead (pass-KV).
vLLM's Decode Context Parallelism \citep{vllm2026dcp} is the
production-engine implementation of the same idea, and
NVIDIA's attention co-design work for interactive long-context
inference \citep{nvidia2026codesign} targets the same regime from the
kernel side. We adopt the pass-Q form under the name \emph{split-KV}
(\S\ref{sec:results-decode}) and contribute a diagnosis of why the
rotation matters as much as it does, plus the measurement of what
removing it is worth on our engine. \textbf{No novelty is claimed for
the technique.}

\paragraph{System-level inference optimization.}
\citet{kwon2023vllm} address GPU memory fragmentation in concurrent
serving. PagedAttention maps KV-cache blocks non-contiguously via
per-sequence block tables, reducing memory waste from 60--80\% to
under 4\% and enabling 2--4$\times$ throughput improvements.
\citet{shoeybi2019megatron} introduced tensor parallelism for
training; \citet{liu2024deepspeedulysses} extended sequence
parallelism to even longer training sequences.

\paragraph{Long-context inference optimization.}
FlashDecoding \citep{dao2023flashdecoding} parallelizes
single-query attention across the KV sequence dimension at decode
time, yielding wall-clock speedups at long context. It is
complementary to RASD: FlashDecoding optimizes the intra-rank
attention kernel while RASD contributes the cross-rank
ring-decode pattern, and the two compose. MInference
\citep{jiang2024minference} accelerates million-token prefill via
dynamic sparse attention patterns identified per attention head.
It is a directly comparable single-device approach to the
million-token capability claim, but targets prefill only and does
not address the autoregressive decode loop that is this paper's
primary subject.

\paragraph{KV quantization.}
KIVI \citep{liu2024kivi} introduced asymmetric per-channel
quantization of K and per-token quantization of V at 2-bit precision.
KVQuant \citep{hooper2024kvquant} pushed this further with
per-channel + non-uniform quantization, demonstrating 10\,M context
on a single A100. NF4 \citep{dettmers2023qlora,dettmers2022bitsandbytes}
is the standard 4-bit data type from the QLoRA line of work. RASD
uses NF4 for the KV cache with a chunked update path and a bf16
outlier-keep prefix on rank 0, drawing on the attention-sink finding
of \citet{xiao2024streamingllm}.

\paragraph{Position scaling.}
Rotary position embeddings \citep{su2024rope} can be extended past
the model's training context through several scaling strategies:
Linear interpolation \citep{chen2023longrope}; NTK-aware
scaling \citep{ntk2023}; YaRN \citep{peng2023yarn}, which combines
NTK with attention-temperature scaling; and LongRoPE
\citep{ding2024longrope}, which searches for the optimal frequency
schedule. RASD uses YaRN where a target needs it. The reviewed version
claimed an 11--18$\times$ perplexity improvement over vanilla RoPE
from the table in \S\ref{sec:results-ppl}; those rows were mislabelled
(they all used factor 8, and the 4\,k row used no scaling at all), and
the two configurations also differ in whether the model is being
asked to work inside or outside its training window, so the
``11--18$\times$'' is \textbf{withdrawn} as a claim about YaRN as
such. What remains is what \S\ref{sec:results-ppl} reports under an
explicit disclosure of the configuration, and the finding that
matters later: scaling can be nearly free in perplexity and
expensive in acceptance (\S\ref{sec:results-rope}).
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E8)

\paragraph{Limitation of prior distributed methods.}
All prior distributed inference work treats the decode step as
strictly sequential: one token is generated per round of KV
communication. At million-token contexts, each inter-GPU KV transfer
step introduces non-trivial latency overhead (order 10--100\,ms on
NVLink, more on PCIe). The expectation in prior work was that this
idle time between communication rounds is structurally
\emph{wasted} --- no useful computation occurs --- and that hiding
it through asynchronous work would yield speedups.

\subsection{Speculative decoding}
\label{sec:related-spec}

\citet{leviathan2023fast} and \citet{chen2023accelerating}
independently introduced speculative decoding: a small draft model
proposes $\gamma$ candidate tokens autoregressively; the large target
model verifies all $\gamma+1$ positions in a \emph{single parallel
forward pass}. The acceptance rule $\min(1, p/q)$ with adjusted
resampling from $\max(0, p-q)/Z$ provably preserves the target
distribution. The expected tokens per large-model call is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spec-tokens}
\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens}] = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1 - \alpha}
\end{equation}
where $\alpha$ is the mean acceptance rate. At $\alpha \approx 0.8$
and $\gamma = 4$, this yields $\approx 3.5$ tokens per large-model
call --- a 2--3$\times$ wall-clock speedup on standard benchmarks
with \emph{provably identical} output quality.

\citet{miao2023specinfer} extended speculative decoding with token
tree verification. \citet{cai2024medusa} attached $K$ additional
decoding heads directly to the target model's frozen hidden state,
eliminating the separate draft model. \citet{li2024eagle} reframed
draft generation as feature-uncertainty modeling. All of these
extensions assume short-to-moderate context regimes; their behavior
at million-token context is not measured in the original papers.

\paragraph{Recent speculative decoding extensions.}
EAGLE-2 \citep{li2024eagle2} introduced dynamic draft trees whose
shape adapts per position based on draft-model confidence, and
EAGLE-3 \citep{li2025eagle3} further improved acceptance through
training-data scaling for the draft head. Both build on the
feature-level drafting of \citet{li2024eagle} and report
wall-clock speedups at short-to-moderate context. These
extensions are directly comparable to RASD's speculative
component and complementary to its central question: this paper
asks what happens to any speculative speedup at million-token
context, which is orthogonal to the choice of draft architecture.

\subsection{Long-context evaluation}
\label{sec:related-eval}

Several benchmarks have emerged for measuring long-context
capability: LongBench \citep{bai2024longbench} (multi-task,
6.7--31\,k contexts), L-Eval \citep{an2023leval} (3--200\,k),
RULER \citep{hsieh2024ruler} (synthetic needle-in-haystack at
arbitrary lengths), and $\infty$Bench
\citep{zhang2024infbench} ($\geq$100\,k). These are
\emph{extrinsic} evaluations of long-context use. This paper
makes \emph{systems} claims (throughput, memory, acceptance) and
treats extrinsic quality eval as out-of-scope, deferred to
follow-up work with a long-context-trained base model. We ship
RULER niah scoring infrastructure with the artifact release for
future work to build on.

\subsection{The research gap and positioning}
\label{sec:related-gap}

The synthesis of these three threads reveals a precise position in
the design space. Ring Attention solves the memory wall but its
decode step is strictly sequential: each layer's key/value shard
must visit every rank before that layer's attention can be
computed. Speculative decoding hides target-model latency but
assumes a single device with idle memory-bandwidth windows ---
not the structured inter-GPU communication windows that arise in
distributed inference. We posited the central question: can the
communication latency of Ring Attention's decode-phase KV rotation
be hidden by the computational work of speculative draft-token
generation?

Mechanistically, the two operations are mutually independent. At
each decode step, the target model must wait for the next KV block
to arrive (cost $\delta_{\text{comm}}$). A draft model that runs for
$\gamma$ steps requires only the \emph{current} KV state, not the
next one. These can run on different CUDA streams. The expected
combined speedup is bounded by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rasd-speedup}
S_{\text{RASD}} \approx
\frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1 - \alpha}
\cdot
\frac{1}{1 + \max\left(0,
\, \tfrac{t_{\text{draft}} - \delta_{\text{comm}}}{t_{\text{verify}}}
\right)}
\end{equation}
which is purely additive ($S \to (1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1})/(1 - \alpha)$)
when the draft phase fits entirely within the communication window
($t_{\text{draft}} \le \delta_{\text{comm}}$).

\paragraph{Positioning of related work.}
Table~\ref{tab:positioning} summarizes how RASD sits in the design
space relative to the closest prior work.

\footnotetext{The reviewed version marked RASD as exploiting decode
overlap. \textbf{That overlap was never implemented}: the draft and the
verify run back to back, and the kernel merely issues the next rotation
before each step's attention (\texttt{prefetch\_depth} 1). The row is
corrected, and the mechanism the paper actually measured is the one

% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E3, E4)

\paragraph{What the measurement did to the hypothesis.}
The reviewed version of this paper answered this question with a
profiler bucket: communication was said to be $\leq 1.2\%$ of wall
time on the speculator rank, so the overlap window was too small to
matter. \textbf{That number is withdrawn.} The bucket recorded
$0.84$/$4.39$/$10.57$\,s at 128\,k/256\,k/512\,k while the physical
wire floor for the same runs is $2.7$/$13.4$/$28.4$\,s: it recorded
$0.31$--$0.37\times$ of the minimum time the link needs to move those
bytes, so it did not capture the transfers and cannot support any
statement about overlap.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E1); results/mlsys/BANDWIDTH_FLOOR.md

What replaces it is a direct measurement of the primitive, and it
reverses the framing. The rotation is not a latency that the draft
work might hide behind: it is the decode step. At 128\,k the ring
performs $8$ rotations $\times$ $32$ layers $=$ \textbf{256 rounds
per decode token}, and a standalone benchmark of the same
\texttt{batch\_isend\_irecv} ring --- no model, 8 ranks, 256 rounds
per payload --- shows each round costs a fixed $\approx$10.3\,ms
\emph{regardless of the payload}: 10.3124\,ms for 4\,KB and
10.3462\,ms for 266\,MB (the K+V of a 128\,k window), a
66\,000$\times$ payload range with a 0.4\% spread and a worst
rank-to-rank spread of 0.056\,ms. The cost is per-round latency, not
bandwidth, and it is paid once per round however small the round is.
The design question is therefore not how to hide the rotation behind
the draft, but how to stop rotating at all --- which is exactly what
prior work in \emph{decode-side context parallelism} does, and
\S\ref{sec:results-decode} measures the consequence of adopting it.
% SRC: results/mlsys/decode_df/ring_bench/ringbench.csv; results/mlsys/DECODE_DIAGNOSIS.md section F

% Section 3 — Methods
% =========================================================================
\section{The RASD System}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Architecture overview}
\label{sec:methods-overview}

Figure~\ref{fig:rasd-topology} shows the ring topology and per-rank
state of RASD on 8 GPUs. Figure~\ref{fig:rasd-decode} shows the
sequence of operations within a single decode round. RASD is an inference loop that runs on $W = 8$
A100 80\,GB SXM4 GPUs on a single node. The target model
(Llama-2-7B) and a smaller draft model (Sheared-LLaMA-1.3B
\citep{xia2023sheared}) are both loaded on every rank, both
quantized to NF4 4-bit weights via
bitsandbytes \citep{dettmers2022bitsandbytes}: the \textbf{weights
are FP4} and the \textbf{KV cache is NF4}. The reviewed version
called the weights NF4 as well; NF4 is the KV codec in this system,
and the distinction matters to anyone reproducing it.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E19)
The KV cache carries a bf16 attention-sink prefix of the first 128
tokens held only on rank 0 (the StreamingLLM construction of
\citet{xiao2024streamingllm}). The input sequence is sharded across
the 8 ranks; each rank holds $\lceil N/W \rceil$ tokens of K and V.
Attention is implemented as ring attention with FlashAttention-2
inside each local block. Rotary position scaling is applied at a
\textbf{fixed factor 8} at every context of 8\,k and above, and
\textbf{not at all} below that; each context is anchored on its own
length rather than on the model's original window, because the
\texttt{transformers} version in use ignores
\texttt{original\_max\_position\_embeddings}. The reviewed version
described a context-dependent factor $f = \lceil N/4096\rceil$
applied consistently; neither half of that was the case.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E7, E8)

The decode loop alternates two phases per round: (i) the draft model
generates $\gamma = 4$ speculative tokens autoregressively on every
rank; (ii) the target model performs a packed forward over those
$\gamma + 1$ positions on all ranks via ring attention, after which
rank 0 broadcasts the draft and target logits to all ranks so that
each rank samples identically (the standard ring-decode invariant). The
acceptance rule of \citet{leviathan2023fast} determines the longest
matching prefix; rejected tokens trigger a residual resample from
$\max(0, p - q)/Z$.

\subsection{Ring-attention sequence parallelism}
\label{sec:methods-ring}

We patch the Llama attention layer at every layer of the target
model. The local-block kernel is FlashAttention-2; the per-round
ring exchange uses \path{torch.distributed.batch_isend_irecv}
for the K and V blocks. Concretely, at decode round $r$:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
    \item Each rank $i$ launches an asynchronous P2P send to rank
          $i-1$ and recv from rank $i+1$ for the $r$-th K/V block.
    \item While that exchange is in flight, the local attention
          kernel computes its contribution to the current query's
          attention output.
    \item The two streams synchronize at the end of the round.
\end{enumerate}
This is the standard Ring Attention decode pattern with one
modification: we add a tick-gate barrier from rank 0 \emph{before}
the \texttt{batch\_isend\_irecv} call to prevent NCCL deadlock at
block sizes $\geq 2048$ at long context.

We chose block size $c = 2048$ as the M3 ablation winner (see
\S\ref{sec:experiments-protocols}). All numbers in this paper use
$c = 2048$.

\subsection{NF4 KV cache with chunked updates and outlier-keep prefix}
\label{sec:methods-nf4}

Three details matter for the memory equation.

\paragraph{(a) NF4 K/V quantization.}
We quantize K and V to 4-bit NF4 \citep{dettmers2023qlora} with a
block size of 32 elements (the inner dimension blocking we found
gave the best acceptance-rate vs.\ memory trade-off in M3
ablations). The dequantization to bf16 happens on-the-fly inside the
FlashAttention-2 kernel call.

\paragraph{(b) Chunked update.}
The naive KV update appends a new $k_i, v_i$ tensor to the cache and
re-quantizes the full per-layer block --- which at 1\,M context
produces a transient bf16 view of the entire layer's KV cache
(several GiB per layer per rank). We split the update into chunks of
2048 elements at a time, keeping the transient under 100\,MiB. This
chunked-update lever is what brings 1\,M-context inference inside
40\,GiB per rank.

\paragraph{(c) Outlier-keep prefix.}
Following the attention-sink finding of
\citet{xiao2024streamingllm}, we keep the first 128 tokens of the
sequence in bf16 on rank 0 only. Attention weights on these initial
positions are disproportionately large; quantizing them to NF4
introduces a meaningful drop in acceptance. The outlier prefix costs
$128 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot L$ bytes on rank 0
$\approx 64\,\text{MiB}$ for the target model --- negligible.

\paragraph{Memory equation.}
Per-rank peak memory at sequence length $N$ over $W$ ranks is
approximately
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:memory}
M_{\text{rank}}(N) \;\approx\;
\underbrace{M_{\text{weights}}}_{\approx 4.0\,\text{GiB}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\frac{N}{W} \cdot L \cdot 2 \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}}_{\text{NF4 KV per rank}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{M_{\text{transient}}}_{\le 4\,\text{GiB}}
\end{equation}
where $L = 32$ layers, $d_{\text{model}} = 4096$ is the hidden width
(32 KV heads $\times$ 128 head dim), and the $\tfrac{1}{2}$
factor is the NF4 4-bit compression ratio relative to bf16. We
use Eq.~\ref{eq:memory} to sketch the dominant terms only: it
does not model transient or scratch contributions that grow with
context --- prefill activations, the FA-2 NF4-dequant scratch, and
the NCCL workspace --- so the measured peak runs ${\sim}15$\,GiB
higher at $N = 10^6$ than these dominant terms account for in
isolation, while still landing inside the per-rank budget
(\S\ref{sec:results-memory}).

\subsection{Speculative verify loop}
\label{sec:methods-spec}

The verify step packs $\gamma + 1$ positions into a single target
forward. Every rank runs the draft model and the packed
$\gamma + 1$-position target forward locally; rank 0 then
broadcasts its draft and target logits to all ranks (a
${\sim}1$\,MB collective per round) so the acceptance test is
bit-identical everywhere, after which every rank samples using a
shared RNG seed. This last point
is load-bearing: the acceptance test
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:acceptance}
\Pr[\text{accept token } t] = \min\Bigl(1, \tfrac{p_{\text{target}}(t)}{p_{\text{draft}}(t)}\Bigr)
\end{equation}
must yield the same answer on every rank so that the KV cache
update is consistent. We verified this invariant with a unit test
(\path{tests/test_verification_math.py}) that runs the verify
loop with two different seeds and confirms byte-identical KV state.

We use $\gamma = 4$ throughout. The M3 ablation grid swept
$\gamma \in \{2, 4, 6, 8, 12\}$ and identified $\gamma = 4$ as the
acceptance/throughput optimum at our draft/target size combination,
agreeing with the moderate-$\gamma$ regime predicted by
\citet{leviathan2023fast}'s analysis.

\subsection{YaRN position scaling}
\label{sec:methods-yarn}

Llama-2 was trained at 4\,k context. To extend to 1\,M we apply
YaRN \citep{peng2023yarn} with factor $f = 256$ (i.e., the model's
position embeddings span $4096 \cdot 256 = 1\,048\,576$ tokens).
YaRN combines NTK-aware $\beta$-scaling of the rotary frequencies
with an attention-temperature factor that depends on $f$.

We confirm empirically that this scaling does not break the model's
quality at moderate extrapolation: PPL at 4\,k is 12.1 and at 8\,k
is 13.2 (essentially flat, see Table~\ref{tab:ppl}). At 32\,k
($f = 8$) PPL rises to 814 --- still interpretable but degraded. We
do not measure PPL at $f \geq 32$ because single-rank PPL evaluation
does not fit at those contexts on 80\,GiB; the YaRN extrapolation
regime is the dominant source of degradation in our long-context
results (\S\ref{sec:results-alpha}).

\subsection{Design-point selection: ablation sweeps}
\label{sec:methods-ablations}

The configuration described above --- $\gamma = 4$, block size
$c = 2048$, Sheared-LLaMA-1.3B draft, prefetch depth 1 --- was not
chosen arbitrarily. Each value is the winner of a one-factor-at-a-
time ablation sweep we ran on a smaller setup (8$\times$A100 40\,GB
SXM4 at 64\,k context) before committing to the full 1\,M-context matrix.
This section reports the five sweeps that fix the design point.
All sweeps reuse 3 seeds $\{42, 123, 456\}$ and report mean
throughput and acceptance (Figure~\ref{fig:ablation},
Table~\ref{tab:m3-ablation}). \textbf{The three seeds are not three
independent samples of anything}: all three ran on the same
synthetic prompt, so they measure run-to-run variation on one input,
not prompt-to-prompt variation. The reviewed version reported a
95\% interval of $\pm 1.96$ standard errors over those three seeds;
at $n=3$ that interval is not meaningful and we report the range and
the $n$ instead wherever a spread is quoted in this paper.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E11, E12)

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{fig2_ablation_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Ablation heatmap across the five design axes (rows) at the
levels swept (columns). Color encodes mean throughput (tok/s) over
3 seeds at 64\,k context. The winning level per axis is annotated
in bold. The block-size sweep (A3) shows the largest single-axis
effect: a 2$\times$ throughput improvement from 256-token blocks to
2048-token blocks at constant acceptance.}
\label{fig:ablation}
\end{figure}

\input{../../tables/ablation_summary.tex}

\paragraph{A1 -- Draft model size.}
We compared TinyLlama-1.1B against Sheared-LLaMA-1.3B as the draft
model. Sheared-LLaMA wins on both throughput (0.87 vs 0.84\,tok/s)
and acceptance (25.3\% vs 23.5\%). The difference is small but
consistent across seeds. We chose Sheared-LLaMA primarily because
its vocabulary is identical to the Llama-2-7B target (avoiding the
tokenizer-mismatch hack required for cross-family pairs), and
secondarily because the modest acceptance gain compounds at higher
$\gamma$. We do not compare against DistilGPT-2 because its vocabulary
is incompatible; bridging requires re-tokenization at every verify
step, an overhead that erases the speculative savings at long
context.

\paragraph{A2 -- Number of speculative steps $\gamma$.}
We swept $\gamma \in \{2, 4, 6, 8, 12\}$ holding all else fixed.
Throughput is approximately flat in $\gamma$ over this range
(0.81--0.86\,tok/s), but acceptance drops monotonically:
$\alpha = 0.38$ at $\gamma = 2$, $\alpha = 0.25$ at $\gamma = 4$,
$\alpha = 0.11$ at $\gamma = 12$. The reviewed version called $\gamma = 4$ the
``acceptance/throughput optimum''. \textbf{Throughput was flat
within noise across the whole sweep} (0.81--0.86\,tok/s), so no
level is an optimum on throughput, and acceptance falls
monotonically with $\gamma$; what the sweep supports is the
\textbf{negative} statement that $\gamma$ is not a throughput lever
in this range at fixed acceptance behaviour, and that larger
$\gamma$ costs acceptance without buying time. We kept $\gamma = 4$
because it is the smallest value the campaign used that does not
leave speculation on the table, and because the later protocol
measurement (Table~\ref{tab:headline}, \S\ref{sec:results-spec})
re-tests draft length under sampling, where the ordering is
different and monotone. Every row here is on the synthetic prompt
and the draft's first-4096 conditioning, so the numbers are
configuration-specific.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E21); results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 8.6

\paragraph{A3 -- KV-cache block size $c$.}
This sweep is the highest-leverage design choice in the paper.
We compared $c \in \{256, 512, 1024, 2048\}$ tokens, where $c$ is the
\textbf{transmission chunk within one rotation} --- the whole shard
moves on every rotation, and $c$ only sets how finely each rotation
is cut. \textbf{The reviewed version defined $c$ as the shard size
and argued that $c = 2048$ was the largest chunk that fits at
1\,M}; that argument is wrong, because the kernel posts every chunk
of a rotation in one batch, so all chunk buffers are live at once and
the memory footprint does not depend on $c$.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E21); src/models/ring_attention_kernel.py
The throughput results are 0.62, 0.87, 1.11, 1.25\,tok/s --- a
\textbf{2$\boldsymbol{\times}$ improvement} ($+102\%$) from the
smallest to largest chunk, with acceptance unchanged (it is
independent of $c$). Larger chunks amortize the fixed per-collective
overhead across more useful work, which is the effect that matters
here; note that this lever is specific to the \emph{ring} decode
path, and it is inert under split-KV, where there is no rotation to
chunk.

\paragraph{A4 -- Prefetch depth (asynchronous overlap).}
The reviewed version compared ``three communication strategies''.
\textbf{There were two}: depth 2 executes the same code path as depth
1 (\path{ring_attention_kernel.py:344}), so the third arm is a
duplicate rather than a measurement. Synchronous exchange against
prefetch-one-ahead is within noise at 64\,k (0.86--0.88\,tok/s), and
prefetch depth 1 was adopted as the default. This knob is neutral at
our scale, and the reviewed version attached to it the wider
conclusion that the overlap budget is not load-bearing. That
conclusion now rests on the direct measurement in
\S\ref{sec:results-decode}, not on this sweep.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E21)

\paragraph{Why the M3 design point transfers to 1\,M.}
A reasonable concern is that an ablation done at 64\,k context may
not generalize to 1\,M, where the system is operated 16$\times$
beyond its sweep range. The transfer arguments are weaker than the
reviewed version made them, and we say why. The block-size winner
($c = 2048$) was justified by memory; that memory argument is now
withdrawn (there is no memory dependence on $c$, see A3), so the
chunk size stands on its throughput effect alone at 64\,k. The
speculative-step choice ($\gamma = 4$) does rest on a per-round
property of the draft-target pair and on the protocol of the run;
the later, sampled measurement of draft length --- the
protocol of this paper, in the project's results record
(\path{results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md} \S8.6: acceptance 0.6558 /
0.4681 / 0.4270 and throughput 0.58904 / 0.71557 / 0.83685\,tok/s at
$\gamma = 2 / 4 / 6$) --- is the one to quote for $\gamma$, and there
the ordering is monotone in throughput and opposite to acceptance.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 8.6 The prefetch-depth arm is neutral at 64\,k and
there is no 64\,k profile, so the reviewed version's
``if communication is 12\% of wall at 64\,k'' is not a measurement
that exists in this paper and \textbf{it is withdrawn}; it also
contradicted the 1.2\% the same version reported elsewhere.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E21)

\paragraph{Design choices we did not sweep.}
The paper reports results on Llama-2-7B. A target-family sweep
(Llama-2-7B vs.\ Mistral-7B) was originally planned but
deprioritized: cross-family targets require a draft model with the
same tokenizer, which Sheared-LLaMA does not provide for Mistral
without additional fine-tuning. Re-running the M3 grid on a
Mistral-Sheared-Mistral-1.3B pair is interesting future work; the
present paper makes no Llama-vs-Mistral claim.

\subsection{Implementation and reproducibility}
\label{sec:methods-impl}

The full system is implemented in PyTorch
2.5.1+cu124 \citep{paszke2019pytorch} on top of the HuggingFace
\path{transformers} library (v4.46.3). We use
bitsandbytes 0.49.2 for NF4 quantization,
\path{flash-attn} 2.8.3 for the local-block kernel, and
\path{wandb} for run logging. All package versions are pinned in
\path{requirements-lock.txt} (frozen at the
\path{m4-phase-c-complete} git tag for the throughput matrix and at
the \path{m3-reablation} git tag\footnote{\url{https://github.com/amankiitg/RASD/releases/tag/m3-reablation}}
for the ablation grid in \S\ref{sec:methods-ablations} ---
the latter captures the post-audit fixes that resolved the
verify-loop defects identified on 2026-04-16).

The repository ships the canonical aggregator
\path{scripts/aggregate_final_results.py} that builds
\texttt{results/final/final\_results.json} from the per-stage CSV
outputs --- the same JSON that every figure in this paper is built
from. We provide reproduction scripts for each experimental stage
(\texttt{scripts/phase\_c\_pod\_session.sh},
\texttt{scripts/phase\_d\_rerun\_session.sh}) plus a 470-test pytest
suite.

% =========================================================================
% Section 4 — Experiments
% =========================================================================
\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Hardware and software}
\label{sec:experiments-hardware}

All measurements were taken on Lambda Cloud
\texttt{gpu\_8x\_a100\_80gb\_sxm4} instances (240 vCPU, 1.8\,TB host
RAM, 8$\times$A100 80\,GB SXM4 connected via NVLink). The software
stack is pinned in \texttt{requirements-lock.txt}: PyTorch 2.5.1
with CUDA 12.4, \texttt{transformers} 4.46.3,
\texttt{accelerate} 0.33.0, \texttt{bitsandbytes} 0.49.2,
\texttt{flash-attn} 2.8.3, \texttt{datasets} 4.8.5, \texttt{wandb}
0.26.1. The Lambda image provides Python 3.10.12 and CUDA 12.8. Two
identically-configured pods were used in sequence: the first ran the
main throughput matrix; the second captured per-position acceptance
traces and saved generations that were not committed from the first
pod. Both pods passed a live-vs-locked
\path{requirements-lock.txt} diff check at bootstrap.

All matrix and sweep runs are publicly logged on Weights \&
Biases\footnote{Project URLs:
\url{https://wandb.ai/amank-iitg-uc-berkeley-electrical-engineering-computer-s/rasd-m4-phase-c}
and
\url{https://wandb.ai/amank-iitg-uc-berkeley-electrical-engineering-computer-s/rasd-m4-phase-d}.
The Reproduction Appendix (\S\ref{app:repro}) maps every figure and
table to its source CSV and the corresponding W\&B run.}.

\subsection{Models, dataset, and prompts}
\label{sec:experiments-data}

\paragraph{Target model.}
Two targets appear in this paper and they are named wherever they
are used. The long-context campaign that produced the throughput
results runs \texttt{gradientai/Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Gradient-1048k},
a model trained to a 1\,M window, so no rotary stretching is
required; the rotary intervention of \S\ref{sec:results-rope} runs
\texttt{meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B}, which ships the
\texttt{rope\_scaling} dictionary under test; and the notation-heavy
ablation sweeps and the HF ceiling test use
\texttt{meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf} \citep{touvron2023llama2}, the
4\,k-window model the system was first built on. All of them are
loaded in bf16 and quantized to FP4 weights with an NF4 KV cache for
inference.
% SRC: results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md section 3e (limitation 4)

\paragraph{Draft conditioning: a correction.}
The draft model in this system is \emph{not} given the whole prompt.
For every run whose prompt exceeded 4096 tokens --- which is every
run in this paper --- the draft was conditioned on the prompt's
\textbf{first 4096 tokens}, not on the tail. The reviewed version
describes the opposite. This is a configuration fact
(\texttt{d89cf41}), it is \emph{disclosed rather than argued}, and it
is the single largest caveat on every acceptance number in this
paper: a draft that cannot see the recent context has to agree with
the target less often, so the absolute acceptance values here are
\emph{lower} than a correctly conditioned draft would give, and the
\emph{contrast} between arms of the rotary intervention
(\S\ref{sec:results-rope}) is unaffected because all arms share the
same conditioning. The 1\,M acceptance numbers are the ones this
matters to most.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E6); commit d89cf41

\paragraph{Protocol of the reported results.}
The results in \S\ref{sec:results} use one protocol. Prompt:\emph{PG-19}
\citep{rae2019pg19} narrative, five books, windowed so that each
rung's scored continuation ends at the same document position as the
1\,M rung, with the cross-rung alignment verified from
\texttt{continuation\_sha256} and the recorded offsets rather than
from the pool's name. Decoding: $T{=}0.7$ sampling, 128 new tokens,
$\gamma{=}4$ speculative steps, draft window cap 4096. Every row is
checked for degeneracy by the detector of \S\ref{sec:results-alpha}
and the check is recorded per row. Speedups are decode-only wherever
they are labelled decode-only, and decode-only means
$(t_{\text{row}} - t_{\text{ttft}})/(\text{tokens} - 1)$: prefill
is excluded, so a decode-path change is not credited with the
prefill it did not touch. Every row records the engine that produced
it (\texttt{ring\_decode\_mode}, the number of patched layers, and
the git commit), so a row that cannot prove its engine is
identifiable and void.

\paragraph{Draft model.}
\path{princeton-nlp/Sheared-LLaMA-1.3B} \citep{xia2023sheared}, at a
pinned revision%
\footnote{Full 40-character commit hash pinned in
\path{requirements-lock.txt}; we abbreviate to \texttt{a4b7693} in
prose.}, NF4-quantized identically to the target. The two models
share a tokenizer.

\paragraph{Dataset and prompt sources.}
We use two prompt sources. (1) \emph{Synthetic repeated-paragraph}
is the default for the throughput matrix: a deterministic
technical-English passage repeated to fill the target context length.
This isolates the system from prompt-content variance. It is also
the prompt that produced the greedy loops of
\S\ref{sec:results-alpha}. The reviewed version described it as
matching ``the protocol used in prior speculative-decoding papers'';
it does not --- those papers evaluate on standard datasets --- and
\textbf{no result in this paper rests on the synthetic prompt}: the
reported protocol is PG-19.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E22) (2) \emph{PG-19}
\citep{rae2019pg19} narrative chunks are used for the perplexity
sanity check at moderate contexts and for the short-context
capability check at 4\,k/8\,k (\S\ref{sec:results-decode}). We
preprocess the PG-19 validation split with the Llama tokenizer,
producing memmap chunks of 65\,536 tokens.

\subsection{Experimental matrix}
\label{sec:experiments-protocols}

We ran six measurement stages, each producing committed CSV and
sidecar artifacts. We use descriptive names below and provide a
direct mapping to the run identifiers used in our public W\&B
projects in Appendix~\ref{app:repro}.

\paragraph{Validation runs.}
Long-context smoke tests at 16\,k--128\,k validated the ring decode
loop and reproduced the per-round acceptance rate $\alpha$ from
prior M3 ablation runs.

\paragraph{Main throughput matrix.}
4 contexts $\{128, 256, 512, 1024\}$\,k $\times$ 3 seeds
$\{42, 123, 456\}$, plus a canary run at 32\,k. Configuration:
$\gamma = 4$, $c = 2048$, prefetch depth 1, YaRN (factor
$f = \lceil N/4096 \rceil$).

\paragraph{Target-only baseline matrix.}
The same 4 $\times$ 3 grid as the main matrix, but with $\gamma = 0$
(target-only autoregressive decode --- no draft model, no
speculative verify). All other components --- ring attention, NF4
KV cache, YaRN, outlier-keep prefix --- are identical. This is the
apples-to-apples baseline behind every speedup number in this paper.

\paragraph{Perplexity sanity check.}
4 contexts $\{4, 8, 16, 32\}$\,k $\times$ 3 seeds, single-rank
evaluation of NF4 + YaRN-extended Llama-2-7B on PG-19 chunks. A
vanilla-RoPE control was run at the same contexts to quantify YaRN's
benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:vanilla-ppl}).

\paragraph{Profiler subset.}
4 contexts $\{32, 128, 256, 512\}$\,k $\times$ 1 seed, each wrapped
in a \texttt{torch.profiler} context to capture per-event timing.
The 1\,M context was attempted but the post-generation aggregation
step (\path{key_averages()}) did not return within 2\,h of CPU
work; we report up to 512\,k and document the limitation in
\S\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Vanilla HF FA-2 ceiling test.}
Single-rank HuggingFace \path{model.generate()} with
\path{attn_implementation=flash_attention_2}, no quantization, no
sequence parallelism. 5 contexts: $\{32, 128, 256, 512, 1024\}$\,k.
This is a \emph{capability} baseline that records the out-of-memory
ceiling of the standard open-source inference stack.

\paragraph{Per-position trace and qualitative re-run.}
The first pod was terminated before we realized that the
per-position acceptance sidecars (\path{*.jsonl} files, one per
verify round) had been excluded by an over-aggressive \path{.gitignore}
rule. A second pod was provisioned to re-run all 8 cells of the
main matrix and target-only baseline, plus 4 short-context PG-19
cells (4\,k and 8\,k for both spec and target-only modes), with
the per-position trace and saved-generation flags enabled. All
sidecars are committed in the artifact release.

\subsection{Metrics}
\label{sec:experiments-metrics}

Following the metric definitions in
Appendix~B of the project roadmap:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
    \item \textbf{Throughput} ($\text{tok}/\text{s}$):
          $T = N_{\text{tokens}} / T_{\text{wall}}$.
    \item \textbf{Latency per output token} (ms):
          $L = (T_{\text{wall}} / N_{\text{tokens}}) \cdot 1000$.
    \item \textbf{Acceptance rate}: $\alpha = N_{\text{accepted}} / N_{\text{drafted}}$
          for $\gamma = 4$. Per-round $\alpha \in \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$.
    \item \textbf{Perplexity}: standard, $\exp(-\tfrac{1}{N}\sum \log P(x_i \mid x_{<i}))$.
    \item \textbf{Time-to-first-token (TTFT)} (ms): wall time from
          \texttt{generate()} entry to the first sampled output token.
          Dominated by prefill cost.
    \item \textbf{Peak GPU memory} (MB): \texttt{nvidia-smi}-reported
          peak across the run, maximum over the 8 ranks.
    \item \textbf{Speedup}: $S = T_{\text{RASD}} / T_{\text{target-only}}$ at matched context.
    \item \textbf{Compute / comm / idle / other (\%)}: rank-0
          time-share buckets from
          \path{torch.profiler.key_averages()}.
\end{itemize}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

% --- 5.1 Capability (RQ1) ---------------------------------------
\subsection{1\,M-token inference on commodity hardware}
\label{sec:results-capability}

We first establish the capability claim. Table~\ref{tab:ceiling}
shows the result of running vanilla HuggingFace
\texttt{Llama-2-7b-hf.generate()} with
\texttt{attn\_implementation=flash\_attention\_2} (bf16 weights,
bf16 KV cache, single rank) at five context lengths. Only the 32\,k
configuration completes; every context $\geq 128\,$k runs out of
memory during the prefill of the input prompt, before any generation
occurs. The 32\,k run consumes 30.1\,GiB of GPU memory and produces
output at 7.25\,tok/s.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Vanilla HuggingFace FA-2 \texttt{generate()} ceiling test.
Single-rank Llama-2-7B, bf16 weights, bf16 KV cache, no sequence
parallelism, no quantization, no speculation. Only ctx=32\,k
completes. ``Peak'' is the maximum GPU memory observed during the
attempt.}
\label{tab:ceiling}
\input{../../tables/main_ceiling.tex}
\end{table}

In the same hardware budget, RASD reaches 1\,M-token context with
\textbf{41.2\,GiB peak allocated per rank} (69\,GiB reserved). The
reviewed version said ``39.3\,GiB peak per rank, half of the
available 80\,GiB''; the reading was \textbf{rank 0 only}, and the
over-rank maxima are the ones quoted here.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E18); results/mlsys/CLAIMS.md C6
\emph{Nominal versus actual context}: the rows reported in this
paper record \textbf{1{,}047{,}551} prompt tokens at the ``1\,M''
rung and \textbf{523{,}263} at ``512\,k'' --- the nominal length less
the 1024-token scored continuation and the current token. The
reviewed version's Llama-2 matrix was built by an older harness that
landed at \textbf{1{,}002{,}984} and 501{,}472 for the same nominal
lengths, which is why quotes of ``1\,M'' differ between the two
halves of the paper unless the builder is named.
% SRC: results/mlsys/rerun_r1/session_a_RR_1M_*.csv (prompt_tokens); results/mlsys/nominal_vs_actual_context.csv
% TODO AMAN: the ceiling test in this subsection is vanilla HF FA-2 on Llama-2-7B
% (bf16), while every throughput result in the paper is on the 1M-native
% gradientai/Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Gradient-1048k target (FP4/NF4). Should we (a) re-run
% the ceiling test on the Llama-3-8B target so the two halves of the paper name the same
% model, or (b) keep it and label the model explicitly in the table caption? I have
% labelled it, but the mismatch remains.
Figure~\ref{fig:throughput} plots throughput against context length
for the three configurations side by side. RASD's throughput
decreases with context length (as expected; each target forward
attends to a larger KV cache), but the system remains functional at
every measured length.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{fig1_throughput_vs_context.pdf}
\caption{Throughput vs.\ context length. RASD spec mode
(\textcolor{blue!70!black}{$\bullet$}) and matched target-only
baseline (\textcolor{orange!90!black}{$\blacksquare$}) at 4 contexts
$\times$ 3 seeds; vanilla HF FA-2 \texttt{generate()}
(\textcolor{green!50!black}{$\blacktriangle$}) at 32\,k only, OOM
markers (\textcolor{red}{$\times$}) for $\geq 128$\,k. Bands are
95\% CI ($\pm 1.96\,$SEM) over 3 seeds. Both axes log scale.}
\label{fig:throughput}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Why HF FA-2 OOMs.}
At ctx=128\,k, the bf16 KV cache alone for Llama-2-7B requires
${\approx} 64$\,GiB; at 1\,M it requires ${\approx} 512$\,GiB. Add
the model weights (${\approx}\,13$\,GiB in bf16) plus prefill activations
(quadratic in sequence length even with FlashAttention's memory
optimization, because each per-row online-softmax pass still
materializes the row's K and V), and a single 80\,GiB A100 cannot
hold the 128\,k working set (model weights $+$ KV cache $+$
activation/scratch buffers), let alone the prefill of a
1\,M-token prompt. RASD shards the KV cache
across $W = 8$ ranks (64\,GiB/rank at 1\,M context) and quantizes
each rank's KV to NF4 (16\,GiB/rank), bringing the per-rank
footprint into the regime where the model weights and transient
buffers fit alongside.

% --- 5.2 Speedup vs target-only baseline (RQ1) ------------------
\subsection{The decode step was the ring's key/value rotation}
\label{sec:results-decode}

The reviewed version of this section reported that the speedup
``regresses to $0.94\times$ at 512\,k and $0.97\times$ at 1\,M'' and
attributed the contraction to base-model behaviour under YaRN
extrapolation. \textbf{Both the number and the attribution are
withdrawn.} The regression is not reproduced by the paper's own
same-code re-run, and the mechanism was never acceptance: decode
tokens per verify round are flat from 256\,k to 1\,M
($1.80$/$1.69$/$1.71$). What moved was the per-round \emph{cost}.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E14)

The cost is the ring's own key/value rotation. At 128\,k each
decode token requires $8$ rotations $\times$ $32$ layers $=$
\textbf{256 rounds} of a \texttt{batch\_isend\_irecv} ring, and
Figure~\ref{fig:ringbench} measures that primitive directly: no
model, 8 ranks, 256 rounds per payload, from 4\,KB to 266\,MB (the
K+V of a 128\,k window). Every payload costs the same
$\approx$10.3\,ms --- the whole range spans $10.3124$--$10.3462$\,ms,
a 66\,000$\times$ payload range with a \textbf{0.4\% spread} and a
worst rank-to-rank spread of 0.056\,ms. A round is therefore
\emph{latency}, not bandwidth, and it is paid once per round however
small the round is. On the same box the profiled ring path spent
${\sim}9.3$\,ms per round, so the bare primitive accounts for the
whole cost of the decode step and leaves nothing to attribute to
per-round engine overhead or rank skew.
% SRC: results/mlsys/decode_df/ring_bench/ringbench.csv; results/mlsys/DECODE_DIAGNOSIS.md section F

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{figD_ring_bench.pdf}
\caption{A bare-process benchmark of the ring primitive the engine
uses (\texttt{batch\_isend\_irecv}, 8 ranks, 256 rounds per payload,
no model). The line is flat: a round costs a fixed $\sim$10.3\,ms
from 4\,KB to 266\,MB, so the ring's decode cost is per-round
\emph{latency} and cannot be amortised by moving more data per
round. Measured on 8$\times$A100 80\,GB SXM4 over NVLink with NCCL
selecting \texttt{P2P/CUMEM/read} on a full NV12 mesh.
% SRC: results/mlsys/decode_df/ring_bench/ringbench.csv
}
\label{fig:ringbench}
\end{figure}

Removing the rotation is prior work --- \emph{decode-side context
parallelism} in the pass-Q/pass-KV sense \citep{meta2024contextparallelism},
vLLM's Decode Context Parallelism \citep{vllm2026dcp}, and the attention
co-design work of \citet{nvidia2026codesign}. We adopt
it under the name \textbf{split-KV}: each rank computes attention for
the (replicated) query against \emph{only its own} prefill shard and
produces a partial output plus a log-sum-exp, and the partials are
merged by one MAX and one SUM \texttt{all\_reduce}; for $q_{\text{len}}=1$
the partials are tiny, and the replicated tail is counted exactly
once. Our contribution here is the measurement, not the technique.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figA_decode_vs_context.pdf}
\caption{Decode time per token against context length, both engines
and both arms, on matched cells. Whiskers are the range over the
cells that both engines measured and $n$ is the number of such cells.
The gap widens with context, which is the signature of a
context-independent per-round cost being removed from a step whose
other terms grow.}
\label{fig:decode-context}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Decode time per token, old ring engine against split-KV, on
\emph{matched} (seed, book) cells --- one value per cell on both
sides, plumbing repeats dropped, the two seed stages hit by the
\S\ref{sec:results-seeds} configuration bug excluded. Speedup is the
ratio of decode-only times, $(t_{\text{row}} - t_{\text{ttft}}) /
(\text{tokens}-1)$.}
\label{tab:headline}
\input{../../results/lcfm/tables/headline.tex}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:headline} is the headline. Decode-only, the fix is
worth \textbf{2.80$\times$ / 3.77$\times$ / 4.37$\times$} with
speculation and \textbf{3.30$\times$ / 4.26$\times$ / 5.32$\times$}
without it, at 128\,k / 512\,k / 1\,M. \textbf{The speedup grows with
context}, which is what a context-independent per-round cost
predicts: as the rest of the decode step grows with the context, the
rotation's fixed 256 $\times$ 10.3\,ms share of it shrinks
\emph{relative} to the rotation-free path that replaces it, so the
ratio improves. That is the mechanistic claim, and it is why the
bare-primitive benchmark matters more than the end-to-end ratio.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.2b; results/mlsys/rerun_r1|r2/session_a_*.csv

Three caveats we state rather than bury. The matched
\emph{old-against-new} comparison is one cell at 512\,k and two at
1\,M, because that is how many books the old engine measured there;
the candidate engine's own target-only denominator is wider --- n=3
books at 512\,k and n=5 at 1\,M after the top-up run of
\S\ref{sec:results-spec} --- which is why the speculation-still-pays
ratios in that subsection are three- and five-book figures while the
speedups in this table remain one- and two-cell ones. And the four arms in the diagnostic that isolated
the mechanism --- \texttt{kv\_block\_size} 32768 ($1.24\times$,
bit-identical token stream) and \texttt{repeat\_kv} after the
rotation ($+2.7\%$, bit-identical) --- are \emph{inert} under
split-KV and carry no claim here; they are reported because they are
what ruled out the cheaper explanations before the rotation itself
was removed.
% SRC: results/mlsys/decode_df/arms/df_arms.csv

\subsection{Speculation still pays on top of the fix}
\label{sec:results-spec}

With the rotation gone, the question the paper started from --- does
speculation still pay at long context? --- can be asked on an engine
whose decode step is no longer dominated by a collective. The answer
is yes: \textbf{$2.01\times$ / $2.29\times$ / $2.20\times$}
decode-only at 128\,k / 512\,k / 1\,M over the same engine's own
target-only path, with three books in the 128\,k spec arm against one
in its target arm, three against three at 512\,k, and five against
five at 1\,M.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md sections 10.2 and 10.7

The two thinnest denominators were topped up after the confirmatory
run, because a speedup whose denominator is one book is a ratio of
one row to another. A dedicated session recorded the three missing
1\,M books (\texttt{train\_915}, \texttt{2204}, \texttt{2768}) and
the two missing 512\,k books (\texttt{train\_1}, \texttt{915}) on the
candidate engine, with the same provenance columns as every other
row. Its 512\,k target-only mean is $2.148$\,s/token over three books
against the $2.346$ single-book value it replaces, and its 1\,M mean
is $3.155$ over five against $3.211$ over two. Both moves are small
and both are downward, so the ratios above are \emph{lower} than the
single-book ones --- which is the direction a thin denominator is
most likely to be flattering in.
% SRC: results/mlsys/rerun_topup/session_a_TP_*.csv; results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.7

End-to-end, where prefill is included, the same comparison reads
$1.95\times$ / $1.76\times$ / $1.41\times$: at 1\,M a row is
$570$\,s of which ${\sim}340$\,s is prefill, so prefill is now the
long pole. Any statement about 1\,M throughput has to say which of the
two it means, and we quote decode-only for the speculation claim.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.2; results/mlsys/rerun_r1/session_a_RR_1M_*.csv

For orientation, the old engine's spec-to-target ratio over the same
rungs was 2.53$\times$ / 2.57$\times$ / 2.37$\times$ on the aligned
sampled pools --- but those are pooled over different book sets and
that engine's rotation cost is inside both arms, so they are not the
figure to quote.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 3

% --- 5.3 Memory scaling ----------------------------------------
\subsection{Memory scaling}
\label{sec:results-memory}

Table~\ref{tab:memory} shows the per-rank peak memory at each
context for both modes. RASD's overhead over target-only is the
Sheared-LLaMA-1.3B draft model plus its own KV cache at the same
context. At 128\,k the overhead is 2.2\,GiB; at 1\,M it shrinks to
0.9\,GiB because the target's KV cache dominates and the draft cache
remains fixed (1.3B parameters with \textbf{FP4} weights --- the
reviewed version said NF4 weights, but NF4 is the \emph{KV} codec in
this system --- are ${\approx} 0.7$\,GiB).
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E19)
The peak per-rank memory at 1\,M, \textbf{41.2\,GiB allocated over
ranks} (69\,GiB reserved; the reviewed version's 39.3\,GiB was rank 0
only), runs ${\sim}15$\,GiB above what the dominant terms of
Eq.~\ref{eq:memory} predict on their own; the gap is attributable
to the transient and scratch buffers we do not model in
\S\ref{sec:methods-nf4} (prefill activations, FA-2 NF4-dequant
scratch, NCCL workspace), and it grows monotonically with context.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E18)

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Per-rank peak memory (GiB) at each context. ``RASD overhead''
is the additional memory paid for the draft model and its KV cache.}
\label{tab:memory}

% --- 5.4 Time breakdown (RQ3) ----------------------------------
\subsection{What the profiler bucket got wrong}
\label{sec:results-profile}

The reviewed version of this section reported that communication was
$1.0$--$1.2\%$ of wall time on the speculator rank and concluded that
overlap masking could not be load-bearing. \textbf{The figure is
withdrawn, and so are the sentences that depended on it.} Two
measured facts decide it:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
  \item The \emph{comm} bucket recorded $0.84$ / $4.39$ / $10.57$\,s
        at 128\,k / 256\,k / 512\,k, while the physical floor for
        moving the same bytes over the same link is
        $2.7$ / $13.4$ / $28.4$\,s. The bucket therefore recorded
        \textbf{$0.31$--$0.37\times$ of the minimum possible time}
        --- it did not capture the transfers. A number below the
        wire floor bounds nothing, and in particular cannot support
        ``issued comm upper-bounds exposed comm, so $\leq 1.2\%$ rules
        out overlap regardless of definition''.
  \item The reported \emph{idle} share is rank 0's time
        \emph{outside \texttt{generate()}'s own timer}: $57$--$80\%$.
        The reviewed text read this as rank 0 waiting on collective
        synchronisation; it is measured outside the region in which
        the collectives happen.
\end{itemize}
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E1, E2); results/mlsys/BANDWIDTH_FLOOR.md

Two further items in this section are corrected rather than
withdrawn. The tick-gate barrier described there is not the code that
produced the throughput numbers in this paper, so it is not discussed
further. And the kernel does issue the next rotation \emph{before}
each step's attention (\texttt{prefetch\_depth} 1); what was never
implemented is the overlap the reviewed version claimed as a design
feature --- the draft generation and the verify pass run back to
back. Table~\ref{tab:profile} is kept only as a record of what was
measured under that profiler configuration.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E3, E4)

% deleting them, on the grounds that a reader of the reviewed version should see the
% bucket and why it is not evidence. Deleting the whole subsection is the alternative;
% say which you prefer.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Time-share breakdown (rank 0, \%) under the reviewed
version's profiler configuration. \textbf{Kept as a record, not as
evidence}: the comm bucket sits below the wire floor for the same
runs, so no conclusion is drawn from it here.}
\label{tab:profile}
\input{../../tables/main_profiler.tex}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.7\linewidth]{fig3_time_breakdown.pdf}
\caption{Stacked-bar time breakdown for rank 0, the configuration
the reviewed version profiled. \textbf{Kept as a record.} The comm

\S\ref{sec:results-decode} replaces it with a direct measurement of
