The mechanism that replaced all of this is the direct measurement in
\S\ref{sec:results-decode}: the rotation is not a cost to be hidden
behind the draft, it is the decode step, and removing it is worth
$2.80$--$5.32\times$.

% --- 5.5 Per-round acceptance (RQ2) ----------------------------
\subsection{Acceptance at long context is measured on degenerate text}
\label{sec:results-alpha}

The reviewed version of this subsection reported a \emph{bimodal}
per-round acceptance distribution at long context, roughly half of
verify rounds rejecting the entire draft, and attributed it to
base-model behaviour under YaRN extrapolation, on the strength of a
short-context PG-19 control. \textbf{The attribution is withdrawn:
the control is confounded.} The 4\,k cells that were used as the
comparison point differ from the long-context cells in at least five
ways at once --- context length, prompt source, prompt content,
position-scaling state, and (see \S\ref{sec:results-seeds}) the
number of tokens the draft was conditioned on --- so nothing about
YaRN follows from it.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E15, E16)

What the same data does support is a measurement hazard, and it is
the more useful finding. Under greedy decoding at long context the
generations degenerate into repetition, and \textbf{a greedy draft
accepts a loop trivially}: when the target is emitting the same
token over and over, the draft's proposal matches, the acceptance
sums to whatever the round structure allows, and the number looks
like a property of the draft's quality. It is not. It is a property
of the text.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 1

We measured the census rather than assuming it. Under greedy, \textbf{9
of 15} long-context rows degenerate under the project's absolute
repetition rule; under sampling at $T{=}0.7$, \textbf{0 of 26} rows
do. Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy} shows the per-row periodic-tail share
--- the favourite statistic of a loop, because a degenerate
generation is $p$-periodic from some token to the end.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 1; results/mlsys/sampling_session/repetition_*.csv

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figC_degeneracy.pdf}
\caption{Periodic tail share per row against the 0.50 ceiling. The
greedy groups (left, middle) are the released rows that carry a
per-row verdict; the sampled group (right) is every sampled row in
the release, old and candidate engines together. The two greedy
groups come from different campaigns and are not pooled: the left
group is the long-context campaign's first-window audit (9 of 10
rows loop), the middle group the later 128\,k temperature arms (1 of
10), and the sampled group contains 1 loop in 83 rows --- the f16
rotary row named in \S\ref{sec:results-rope}, which is why the
rotary-table caveat exists. The manuscript's long-context census
quoted in the text (9 of 15 at long context) is the campaign's own
audit; its per-row sidecars are not part of this release.}
\label{fig:degeneracy}
\end{figure}
% TODO AMAN: the figure's greedy groups are the two campaigns whose per-row verdicts are
% in the release (9 of 10, and 1 of 10), while the text quotes the campaign's own
% long-context census (9 of 15), whose per-row sidecars are not released. I have made the
% caption say exactly that rather than forcing the two to agree. If you would rather the
% figure match the text, the 1M greedy sidecars would have to be recovered from the
% October pod and re-scored; say the word and I will try, but it is a compute task.

Three consequences, all of them applied in this paper rather than
merely noted:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
  \item \textbf{The headline matrix is sampled at $T{=}0.7$.} Every
        campaign after the repetition stop uses sampling, and the
        earlier greedy numbers are reported separately and labelled
        rather than averaged in.
  \item \textbf{Every row is checked for degeneracy rather than
        assumed clean}, with the check recorded per row. Where a row
        does trip a ceiling it is reported by name, not smoothed
        away. In the sampled pools, longest verbatim repeat span is
        8 tokens against a 128-token ceiling and the share of tokens
        inside a repeated 16-gram is 0.00 against a 0.60 ceiling.
  \item \textbf{A temperature ablation points up, not down}: at
        128\,k, $T{=}1.0$ gives acceptance 0.7369 against 0.4681 at
        the headline $T{=}0.7$ ($+57\%$ relative, and on five of five
        books), with 0 of 5 rows degenerate in both arms. Greedy
        ($T{=}0.0$) is \emph{worse} than the headline once its one
        looping row is set aside (0.3818 against 0.4681), and the
        looping row is what was holding its mean up.
\end{enumerate}
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md sections 1 and 8.5

\subsection{A configuration bug and the corrected baseline}
\label{sec:results-seeds}

Two stages of the seed ablation --- the ones that were supposed to
run seeds 123 and 456 at 1\,M --- ran seed 42 instead. The cause is
in the harness, not the engine: the config builder merges a level
into the defaults and then sets the run's seed from the
\emph{defaults'} \texttt{seeds} list, so a level that declares its
own \texttt{seeds} has it recorded and then overwritten
(\path{run_experiment.py:590-612}, where the comment explains that
the rule was written because ``greedy decoding makes a seed change a
no-op''). The rows it produced are not wrong, but their run ids say
something untrue about their seed, and every old-engine pool that
contained them inherited that.
% SRC: results/mlsys/CLAIMS.md C15; results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.3

\textbf{What is corrected.} The old-engine 1M baseline is rebuilt
from rows that were never affected: seed 42 from the sampling
session, seeds 123 and 456 from the dedicated corrected run. On the
\textbf{13 matched (seed, book) cells}:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
  \item the 1\,M spec speedup is \textbf{4.375$\times$}, not
        $4.033\times$;
  \item the 1\,M acceptance difference is \textbf{$-0.1\%$}, not
        $-10.4\%$ --- i.e. \textbf{the candidate engine's acceptance
        is unchanged}, and the previously reported drop was an
        artefact of comparing one old-engine seed against three
        candidate seeds;
  \item the old engine's own seed spread is \textbf{23.0\%} of the
        mean on the matched books, so the candidate's per-seed
        movement ($-15.7\%$ / $+10.9\%$ / $+11.3\%$) is \emph{inside}
        the old engine's own seed-to-seed variation, in both
        directions.
\end{itemize}
Both withdrawn claims --- ``the old engine's acceptance is identical
across seeds'' and ``these are the first real 1M seed replicates'' ---
came from the bugged rows and are removed everywhere.
% SRC: scripts/mlsys_seed_baseline_audit.py; results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.3

\textbf{Why the token streams still matter.} That split-KV leaves
acceptance unchanged is not an accident to be waved through: an
exactly-equivalent kernel can still move an acceptance number,
because the accept/reject decision compares the target's distribution
against the draft's proposal, so one flipped near-tie changes the
emitted prefix and every later proposal with it. We checked the
kernel directly. The target-only stream under split-KV is
\textbf{bit-identical to the ring baseline for twelve consecutive
tokens} and diverges at a step where the baseline's own top-2 logit
margin is \textbf{0.0000} (that row's median margin is 2.9375); the
perplexity of the same prefill is identical to six decimals. The
speedups measured here are therefore not bought with a different
model.
% SRC: results/mlsys/DECODE_DIAGNOSIS.md sections F.4/F.5; results/mlsys/decode_df/arms/df_arms.csv

\textbf{One process failure recorded rather than hidden.} The rerun
gate carried a rule that a first-token time differing from the old
engine by more than 10\% would stop the run. Speculation's TTFT came
in 13.0\% below the old engine's and the stop was overridden by
judgement: the old engine's own 128\,k spec TTFT spans
8.397--12.368\,s (sd 0.958), so a 10\% band is not resolvable at that
n; the candidate's two runs of the same prefill differ by 19\% on
their own; and target-only, where prefill alone is measured, matches
the old engine to +1.2\%. The numbers are recorded so a reader can
disagree with the call.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.6

% TODO AMAN: this subsection puts the unflattering decode ratio (our decode is
% 130-162x slower per token than vLLM's) in the same table as our favourable prefill
% ratio. I think a camera-ready must carry both, and the alternative --- showing only
% the end-to-end numbers, where we are ahead at 512k and 1M --- is the kind of selection
% this revision exists to undo. Confirm you want both.
\subsection{Comparison against a production engine}
\label{sec:results-vllm}

We benchmark vLLM 0.6.3 (TP=8) on the same prompts, fed the same
token ids from our own sidecars (\texttt{unit\_matched} on every
row), and the comparison is \textbf{not precision-matched}: vLLM runs
\textbf{bf16 weights with a bf16 KV cache and greedy decoding}, RASD
runs \textbf{FP4 weights with an NF4 KV cache}, $T{=}0.7$ sampling
and speculation. Every ratio below carries that mismatch.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{vLLM (bf16, bf16 KV, greedy) against the ring engine and
the split-KV engine (FP4 weights, NF4 KV, $T{=}0.7$ sampled) on the
same prompts. Prefill is the first-token time; decode is per token.
\textbf{Not a precision-matched comparison} --- the two systems
differ in precision and in sampling.}
\label{tab:vllm}
\input{../../results/lcfm/tables/vllm.tex}
\end{table}

Two readings that point in opposite directions, and both belong in
the paper:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
  \item \textbf{Our prefill beats vLLM's entire run} --- its prefill
        plus its 128 decode steps --- by 1.92$\times$ / 2.52$\times$ /
        2.56$\times$ at 128\,k / 512\,k / 1\,M. This is a property of
        the ring prefill, is untouched by split-KV, and is the
        strongest end-to-end statement this paper can make against a
        production engine.
  \item \textbf{vLLM's decode is 130--162$\times$ faster per token
        than ours} even after the fix, against 429--731$\times$
        before it. Removing the rotation eliminated roughly 70\% of
        the decode deficit and left RASD's decode far behind a
        production engine. The honest framing is that the ring's
        rotation was the \emph{decode pathology} and that removing it
        made our decode merely slow --- not competitive.
        Speculative decoding does not close the gap: our spec decode
        is 65$\times$ / 65$\times$ / 59$\times$ vLLM's.
\end{itemize}
% SRC: results/mlsys/vllm_run2/vllm_baseline.csv; results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md section 3d

End-to-end, with prefill included, the split-KV engine is
0.23$\times$ / 1.09$\times$ / 1.66$\times$ of vLLM at the three
contexts: the ordering flips with context because prefill dominates
at 1\,M and decode at 128\,k.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.5

\subsection{Quality: quantization, rotary stretching, and coherence at 1\,M}
\label{sec:results-ppl}

A quality reviewer's first question on a system paper using a
quantized weight format and rotary position scaling is: ``how much
did you degrade the model?'' We answer it in three parts: a
quantization sanity check, the rotary intervention (F1), and a
coherence check at 1\,M on a natively long-context target (F3).

\paragraph{Configuration disclosure.} The reviewed version of the
table below labelled its rows by intent; the engine's actual
configuration differed in two ways that are disclosed here for the
first time. \textbf{Every row at 8\,k and above used rotary scaling
at a fixed factor 8}, not $\lceil N/4096 \rceil$: the factor was a
configuration value rather than a function of the context length.
And \textbf{every row at 8\,k and above was anchored on its own
context length}, not on the model's original window, because the
\texttt{transformers} version in use ($\leq$4.50) ignores
\texttt{original\_max\_position\_embeddings}. At 4\,k the engine
applies \textbf{no rotary scaling at all}, so the 4\,k row is a
vanilla-RoPE row rather than a scaled one.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E7, E8, E9)
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Perplexity (3-seed mean) of NF4-quantized Llama-2-7B on
PG-19 validation chunks, with and without rotary position scaling.
At 4\,k the engine applies no scaling; at 8\,k and above every row
uses \textbf{factor 8} anchored on its own context length (see the
disclosure above). The ``benefit'' column is the perplexity ratio of
vanilla to scaled --- the gain in quality from scaling. PPL beyond
32\,k requires a ring-SP forward and is deferred
(\S\ref{sec:limitations}).}
\label{tab:ppl}
\input{../../tables/main_ppl.tex}
\end{table}

\paragraph{The quantized model is not quant-broken.}
At Llama-2's native 4\,k context, PPL is 12.1 under scaling and 10.7
under vanilla rotary. We would like to anchor that level against a
published unquantized figure and we cannot: the reviewed version
attributed a 7--12 PG-19 perplexity range to the Llama-2 report
\citep{touvron2023llama2}, and no PG-19 perplexity appears there.
The citation is \textbf{withdrawn} and the number is reported as
measured. What the two 4\,k rows do establish is that the gap
between them is the \emph{rotary} cost at the model's own training
context, not a quantization cost: both rows are quantized
identically.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E22)

\paragraph{Scaling is a large win at moderate extrapolation.}
At 8\,k (2$\times$ the training window), vanilla rotary collapses to
PPL=149 while the scaled configuration stays at PPL=13. At 16\,k,
vanilla=1527 against 85. At 32\,k, vanilla=3895 against 814. The
11--18$\times$ improvement at 8\,k--16\,k justifies scaling over none.
That the 32\,k figure is 814 is the honest limit of the arrangement:
we do not claim quality preservation at 32\,k, only at the native
4\,k context, and the long-context degradation of this base model is
a property of the model and the arrangement rather than of the
system.

\subsection{Rotary stretching: perplexity and acceptance dissociate}
\label{sec:results-rope}

The reasoning above invites an inference that turns out to be false:
that a position-scaling intervention which costs little in
\emph{perplexity} will cost little in \emph{acceptance}, because the
draft and the target see the same positions. We tested it directly
on \texttt{meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B}, a model that \emph{ships} the
\texttt{rope\_scaling} dictionary the intervention modifies, so the
change is applied by the model's own configuration path rather than
by a patch, and on the same book, seed, temperature,
\texttt{spec\_steps} and token budget in all three arms --- the arms
differ in \textbf{nothing} but \texttt{rope\_factor}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{The rotary intervention at 128\,k on
\texttt{meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B}: five books per arm, seed 42, FP4
weights with an NF4 KV cache. Acceptance is the speculative
acceptance rate; the perplexity ratio is the paired measurement
against the native arm on the same continuation. The \texttt{tok/s}
column is \textbf{old-engine} throughput and is reported for
completeness only: the finding is the acceptance and perplexity
contrast, and no speedup is claimed from these arms.}
\label{tab:rope}
\input{../../results/lcfm/tables/rope.tex}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figB_rope.pdf}
\caption{Left: speculative acceptance per arm, with the five books
drawn as points so the direction can be checked per book rather than
only in the mean. Right: the paired perplexity ratio against the
native arm. Stretching the rotary basis costs 0.05\% and 1.56\% of
perplexity and 27\% and 31\% of acceptance.}
\label{fig:rope}
\end{figure}

Acceptance falls from \textbf{0.7272} (native) to \textbf{0.5336}
(factor 16) and \textbf{0.5006} (factor 32) --- a \textbf{27--31\%
relative loss} --- while the paired perplexity ratio moves by
\textbf{+0.05\%} and \textbf{+1.56\%}. The direction holds on five of
five books individually, so this is not a book-specific effect.
Because the three arms differ in nothing else, the drop is a
\textbf{rotary effect at n=3 arms}: not an artefact of the draft, the
target, the book or the seed.
% SRC: results/mlsys/sampling_session/session_a_ROPE_SAMP_{NATIVE,F16,F32}_SPEC.csv; session_a_rope_fix_gate.csv

The two stretched factors land far closer to each other (0.5336 and
0.5006, 6.6\% apart) than either lands to native (27\% and 31\%),
which is what a saturating intervention looks like. At n=3 books the
two stretched factors were within 0.0012 of each other and that was
read as exact saturation; at n=5 they are 0.033 apart, so the
specific 0.0012 is \textbf{withdrawn} and the claim becomes the
weaker, still-supported one: both stretched factors sit far from
native and near each other.
% SRC: results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md F1 (caveats iii-iv)

\paragraph{Why this matters for the technique.} A speculative decoder
is only as good as the agreement between the draft's proposal
distribution and the target's. Position scaling is normally evaluated
by perplexity, and by that measure it is nearly free here --- 1.56\%
for a factor-32 stretch. The same intervention costs almost a third
of the acceptance, and therefore almost a third of the speculation
speedup, and \emph{nothing in the perplexity number reveals it}.
Acceptance under any change to the target's positional treatment must
be measured, not inferred.

One caveat that scopes the claim: every arm here ran on the
\textbf{old engine}, so the absolute acceptance levels sit on the
pre-fix decode path. The \emph{contrast} is unaffected, because
split-KV does not change which tokens are generated
(\S\ref{sec:results-seeds} checks this directly). No rotary arm has
been run under the candidate engine.

\subsection{Coherence at 1\,M on a natively long-context target}
\label{sec:results-coherence}

The perplexity table above cannot reach 1\,M: a single-rank forward
does not fit. This subsection does the long-context version of the
same check on a target trained to 1\,M
(\texttt{gradientai/Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Gradient-1048k}), where no
stretching is required and the question is simply whether the model
is still a model at 1\,M. The rungs are matched by
\texttt{continuation\_sha256} and by the recorded window offsets ---
never by the pool's name --- because scoring a different continuation
at 1\,M would make the comparison meaningless.

On the \textbf{one exactly aligned book} the target's own perplexity
is \textbf{1.805 at 1\,M} against \textbf{1.649 at 128\,k}, i.e.
\textbf{+9.5\%}. On the two books that share 91--95\% of their scored
tokens the difference is within \textbf{1.1\%}. A natively
long-context target therefore does stay coherent across an 8$\times$
context increase, which is the property the long-context campaign
depends on; but the strongest form of that claim rests on \emph{one}
exactly aligned book, and we say so rather than pooling the three and
reporting a tighter number.
% SRC: results/mlsys/sampling_session/QUALITY_FIX_1M_* vs QUALITY_FIX_128K_*; alignment.csv

These measurements are prefill-only (\texttt{measure\_target\_ppl}
scores a forward pass with \texttt{use\_cache=False}), so split-KV
cannot move them: the numbers are identical under both engines. The
engine used is therefore not a caveat here.
% SRC: results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md F3

% --- 5.7 Qualitative comparison --------------------------------
\subsection{Qualitative comparison: RASD vs.\ target-only}
\label{sec:results-qual}

A final sanity check: speculative decoding preserves the target
distribution by construction
\citep{leviathan2023fast,chen2023accelerating}, so RASD's outputs
should match what target-only would produce. Table~\ref{tab:qual}
shows side-by-side excerpts of the final $\sim$200 characters of
generated text for each of the six (context $\times$ prompt-source)
configurations. Both systems used seed=42 and saw identical input
prompts.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\caption{Qualitative continuations: RASD vs.\ target-only at six
configurations, last $\sim$200 characters of generated text.
At 4\,k--8\,k (PG-19) both systems produce English-like
continuations; at long contexts (synthetic prompt + YaRN
factor 32--256) both produce equivalent degenerate text. RASD does
\emph{not} collapse the generation distribution; the base model is
the limit. Generations elided to \texttt{[\ldots]} for length.}
\label{tab:qual}
\input{../../tables/qualitative_examples.tex}
\end{table}

Two observations.

\paragraph{In the well-behaved regime, RASD and target-only diverge.}
At ctx=4\,k and ctx=8\,k with PG-19 prompts, RASD and target-only
generate \emph{different} continuations --- both English-like, both
plausible per-token, but not character-for-character identical. This
is expected: speculative decoding samples from the same target
distribution but with different RNG consumption patterns
(see the resample step in Eq.~\ref{eq:acceptance}). The fact that
both produce coherent English continuations confirms that RASD is
not producing a degenerate or simplified output relative to
target-only.

\paragraph{At long context, both systems degrade equivalently.}
At ctx=128\,k--1\,M with the synthetic repetitive prompt and YaRN
factor 32--256, both RASD and target-only produce near-random tokens
(e.g., \texttt{".W8: ????? Gal!BVICE QO[...]}", where ? marks
non-ASCII glyphs in the original output). This is
not a RASD bug --- it is the Llama-2 + YaRN extrapolation regime
discussed in \S\ref{sec:results-alpha} and \S\ref{sec:results-ppl},
manifesting in the generated text. The two systems agree on the
\emph{quality} of the output (both equivalently degenerate), which
is the consistency property we wanted to confirm.

% =========================================================================
% Section 6 — Discussion and Limitations
% =========================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Sample size per cell is small and we state it everywhere.}
The 128\,k arm has 3 matched spec cells and 1 target-only cell;
512\,k has 3 and 1; 1\,M has 13 and 2. Those are the \emph{matched}
old-against-new cells. Within the candidate engine, where nothing has
to be matched, the target-only arms are 1, 3 and 5 books at 128\,k,
512\,k and 1\,M. Speeds are quoted decode-only for the
comparisons that move through the decode path and end-to-end where
prefill is what dominates. Where a cell has $n=5$ the five units are
books, not seeds: the book-to-book spread (2.3$\times$ in decode rate;
0.30--0.68 acceptance at 1\,M) is larger than the seed-to-seed spread
(1.04$\times$), so five books and five seeds are not interchangeable
and we never claim both.
% SRC: results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md section 3e (limitation 1); RESULTS_OCT.md 10.3

\paragraph{One node, one interconnect, one precision.}
Every measurement is on a single 8$\times$A100 80\,GB SXM4 node over
NVLink with a full NV12 mesh. Multi-node ring attention moves the
collective to a slower fabric and is the regime in which per-round
latency --- the thing \S\ref{sec:results-decode} measures --- would
grow, so nothing here transfers to it without measurement. And there
is \textbf{no bf16 row}: every number is FP4 weights with an NF4 KV
cache, so the precision cost is inside every number, and the vLLM
comparison in \S\ref{sec:results-vllm} is explicitly not
precision-matched.
% SRC: results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md section 3e (limitations 2-3)

\paragraph{One target family, one corpus.}
The camera-ready results are on Llama-3-8B targets (see
\S\ref{sec:experiments-data}) and PG-19 narrative text. The rotary
intervention is on a different model on purpose --- it needs a model
that ships the \texttt{rope\_scaling} dictionary --- but that means
the two findings are on two families, and neither establishes
anything about other architectures or other corpora.

\paragraph{The draft saw the prompt's first 4096 tokens.}
This is the largest caveat on the acceptance numbers
(\S\ref{sec:experiments-data}). It biases the \emph{level} of
acceptance downward on every run with a prompt longer than 4096
tokens, and it does not affect the \emph{contrasts} between arms that
share the conditioning.

\paragraph{Acceptance under split-KV is explained, not tested.}
The 1\,M acceptance is unchanged ($-0.1\%$ over 13 matched cells)
while per seed it moves both ways ($-15.7\%$ / $+10.9\%$ / $+11.3\%$)
inside an old-engine seed spread that is itself 23.0\% of the mean.
The mechanism we offer --- one flipped near-tie changes the emitted
prefix and with it every later proposal --- is consistent with every
measurement but was not tested directly; the direct test would hold
the emitted prefix fixed and re-measure the decision.
% SRC: results/mlsys/RESULTS_OCT.md section 10.3

\paragraph{1\,M prefill is now the long pole.}
A candidate-engine 1\,M row takes 570\,s of which 335\,s is prefill,
so the end-to-end speedup at 1\,M is 1.42$\times$ even though
decode-only is 2.25$\times$. Any claim about 1\,M throughput has to
say which of the two it means, and the next optimisation at 1\,M is
the prefill, not the decode step this paper fixed.
% SRC: results/lcfm/CAMERA_READY_KIT.md section 3e (limitation 7)

\paragraph{An unattributed elementwise term.}
In the profiled 128\,k decode window, 19.3\% of device time was
elementwise kernels --- casts, dequantisation, softmax bookkeeping ---
that were never attributed to a specific operation. With the rotation
gone this is a \emph{larger} share of what remains, and it is the most
obvious next optimisation on the decode path.
% SRC: results/mlsys/DECODE_DIAGNOSIS.md section C

\paragraph{Two withdrawn claims are recorded, not deleted.}
A reader of the reviewed version needs to know they are gone: the
``communication is $\leq 1.2\%$ of wall'' result, whose bucket
recorded $0.31$--$0.37\times$ of the physical wire floor, and the
$4.4\times$ ``native context'' speedup, which was one pair from one
session on a control that differs from the long-context cells in at
least five ways at once. Neither is used anywhere above.
% SRC: results/mlsys/LCFM_RECONCILE.md (AUDIT E1, E16)

% =========================================================================
% Section 7 — Conclusion
% =========================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We asked whether speculative decoding's short-context speedup
transfers to million-token inference, and the answer turned out to
depend on something other than speculation. Under greedy decoding the
acceptance numbers at long context are measured on degenerate text
--- 9 of 15 long-context rows loop, and a greedy draft accepts a loop
trivially --- so the campaign was re-run under sampling, where 0 of 26
rows loop. On that protocol, stretching the rotary basis of a model
that is out of distribution at the target context costs $+0.05\%$ to
$+1.56\%$ of perplexity and \emph{27--31\% of acceptance}: acceptance
and perplexity dissociate, and the second is not a proxy for the
first. A natively 1\,M-trained target, by contrast, stays coherent at
1\,M (within 9.5\% of its 128\,k perplexity on the exactly aligned
book), so the long-context regime is not intrinsically hostile to
speculation.

What \emph{was} hostile was our own engine. Rotating each layer's
key/value shard around eight ranks costs 256 rounds per decode token,
and a bare-process benchmark of the ring primitive shows each round
costs a fixed $\approx$10.3\,ms whatever the payload --- 4\,KB and
266\,MB within 0.4\% of each other, across a 66\,000$\times$ range.
The decode step was latency per round, and the fix was not to hide
that latency behind the draft but to stop rotating: adopting
decode-side context parallelism (prior work) removes 256 rounds per
token and is worth \textbf{2.80$\times$ / 3.77$\times$ / 4.37$\times$}
decode-only with speculation and \textbf{3.30$\times$ / 4.26$\times$ /
5.32$\times$} without it, growing with context as a
context-independent per-round cost predicts. Speculation still pays
$2.0$--$2.3\times$ on top, and widening the two thinnest
target-only denominators from one and two books to three and five
moved that figure by less than the book-to-book spread.

The same measurement disciplines the comparison that matters most
honestly: against vLLM at bf16 and greedy decoding, our prefill beats
that engine's entire run by 1.92--2.56$\times$, and its decode is
still 130--162$\times$ faster per token than ours even after the fix
(it was 429--731$\times$ before). The ring's rotation was the decode
pathology; removing it made our decode merely slow. That is the
honest systems claim, and it is the one this paper makes.

Arriving at any of this required a system that can run a
target-model forward at 1\,M context on commodity hardware. RASD
combines ring-attention sequence parallelism, an NF4 KV cache with
chunked updates and a bf16 outlier-keep prefix, rotary position
scaling where the target's horizon requires it, and speculative
verification with a small draft model. On 8$\times$A100 80\,GB SXM4
it runs a 1\,M-native target at 1\,M context with 41.2\,GiB peak
allocated per rank, where the standard HuggingFace stack runs out of
memory at 128\,k single-rank.

\paragraph{Future work.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt]
    \item \textbf{Fix the draft's conditioning.} The draft should see
          the recent window, not the prompt's first 4096 tokens.
          Every acceptance number in this paper is a lower bound
          until that is done, and the re-measurement is cheap.
    \item \textbf{Attack the elementwise term.} 19.3\% of decode
          device time is unattributed elementwise work, now a larger
          share of what remains after the rotation was removed.
    \item \textbf{The prefill is the 1\,M pole.} A 1\,M row is 335\,s
          of prefill against 235\,s of decode; the decode-side fix
          has moved the bottleneck, and the next one is on the
          prefill path.
    \item \textbf{Multi-node, and larger $W$.} Per-round ring latency
          is what this paper measured on NVLink; on InfiniBand it
          should be worse and the same benchmark applies unchanged,
          which makes it the natural next measurement rather than a
          new system.
\end{itemize}

We release the implementation under MIT license with the
reproduction scripts, the per-position traces, every saved
generation, per-rank memory snapshots, and the CSVs behind every
number in this paper.

\section{Vanilla-RoPE Perplexity (methodology baseline)}
\label{app:vanilla-ppl}

The YaRN-vs-vanilla PPL comparison reported in
\S\ref{sec:results-ppl} (Table~\ref{tab:ppl}) is grounded in two
matched 12-row CSV files at
\path{results/perplexity/m4_ppl_vanilla_rope.csv} and
\path{results/perplexity/m4_ppl.csv}. Both are 3 seeds
$\{42, 123, 456\} \times $ 4 contexts $\{4{,}096; 8{,}192; 16{,}384;
32{,}768\}$ on PG-19 chunks, single-rank, NF4-quantized
Llama-2-7B. The two files differ only in \texttt{rope\_type}:
vanilla rotary (no scaling) vs.\ a \textbf{fixed factor 8} anchored
on each context's own length --- \emph{not} the context-dependent
$\lceil N/4096\rceil$ the reviewed version described, and at 4\,k the
engine applies no scaling so that row is the vanilla row in both
files (AUDIT E8). 3-seed mean PPLs are: vanilla --- 10.7, 149, 1527,
3895; YaRN --- 12.1, 13, 85, 814 at the same contexts. The
$11$--$18\times$ improvement at $8\,$k--$16\,$k that motivates
adopting YaRN is computed as the ratio of these per-context
3-seed means. The control run was deliberately limited to
contexts that fit single-rank without ring-SP forward (the
$\leq 32\,$k cap), so the scaling benefit at $\geq 64\,$k is not
measured here. The long-context quality evidence in this paper is
\emph{not} an extrapolation of this table: it is the direct coherence
measurement of \S\ref{sec:results-coherence} on a natively
long-context target, and the rotary-acceptance dissociation of
\S\ref{sec:results-rope}. The reviewed version inferred a
rate-limiter for long context from this 4\,k--32\,k table; that
inference is withdrawn (AUDIT E15).

\section{RULER Needle-in-Haystack Infrastructure (deferred eval)}
\label{app:ruler}

We built the RULER niah single-needle harness as part of the
benchmark surface and stopped short of running the full eval
in this paper. The infrastructure is committed at
\path{scripts/score_ruler_niah.py} (a stand-alone scorer that
reads paired \path{<run_id>.ruler_niah.json} +
\path{<run_id>.generated.txt} sidecars and emits a CSV of
\texttt{found / not found} per run), with the prompt builder
exposed via the \texttt{--prompt-source ruler\_niah} flag in the
main inference driver. What is missing is the run grid: a
defensible RULER report needs $\sim$50--100 needle positions per
context and at least 3 seeds, which at the 6 contexts we report
inflates to 1{,}000+ generations. The compute budget was prioritized for the
throughput diagnosis and its confirmation; the wiring is left in
place so that a follow-up run needs no further engineering. This
appendix is \emph{infrastructure only} and supports no claim in this
paper.

\section{Evidence Tree}
\label{app:full-results}

Every number in this paper traces to a committed CSV or sidecar.
The tree is organised by claim rather than by file type, and the
pools used for the headline numbers are listed with the rows they
exclude, because two of them had to be excluded after the fact.

\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{Throughput and speedup (F4, F5)} ---
        \path{results/mlsys/rerun_r1/session_a_*.csv} and
        \path{rerun_r2/session_a_*.csv} (31 ok rows; each records
        \texttt{ring\_decode\_mode}, the patched-layer count and the
        git commit, so a row that cannot prove its engine is
        identifiable and void).
  \item \textbf{Old-engine baseline} ---
        \path{results/mlsys/sampling_session/session_a_SAMP_*.csv},
        \path{results/mlsys/fp4_seeds/session_a_FP4_SEED_1M_SPEC.csv}
        and the n=5 extension in
        \path{results/mlsys/n5_extension/}. The two stages hit by the
        configuration bug (\texttt{SA\_SEED\_123\_1M\_SPEC},
        \texttt{SA\_SEED\_456\_1M\_SPEC}) are excluded by name in
        \path{scripts/mlsys_seed_baseline_audit.py}, which prints the
        exclusion list and the matched-cell table.
  \item \textbf{Rotary intervention (F1)} ---
        \path{session_a_ROPE_SAMP_*_SPEC.csv} plus
        \path{ROPE_EXT_SAMP_*} (five books per arm) and the paired
        perplexity ratios in \path{session_a_rope_fix_gate.csv}.
  \item \textbf{Degeneracy (F2)} --- the per-stage
        \path{repetition_*.csv} files, one row per run, produced by
        \path{scripts/mlsys_repetition_report.py} from the token
        sidecars. Where no such CSV exists the row is scored from the
        sidecar by the same module, so the rule is one implementation
        rather than three.
  \item \textbf{Coherence (F3)} ---
        \path{QUALITY_FIX_{128K,1M}_*} with
        \path{results/mlsys/sampling_session/alignment.csv} carrying
        the per-book offsets and continuations hashes.
  \item \textbf{Decode diagnosis} ---
        \path{results/mlsys/decode_df/ring_bench/ringbench.csv}
        (bare ring, five payloads, per-rank) and
        \path{results/mlsys/decode_df/arms/df_arms.csv} (four engine
        configurations in one load, with per-row provenance); the
        argument and the correctness evidence are written up in
        \path{results/mlsys/DECODE_DIAGNOSIS.md} section F.
  \item \textbf{Profiler configuration} --- the reviewed version's
        traces, kept as a record only: the comm bucket in them is
        below the physical floor for the same runs
        (\S\ref{sec:results-profile}).
  \item \textbf{vLLM reference} ---
        \path{results/mlsys/vllm_run2/vllm_baseline.csv} (bf16,
        bf16 KV, greedy, \texttt{unit\_matched} on every row). The
        earlier run at \path{results/mlsys/vllm_run/} is retained but
        its first-token and decode clocks are absolute monotonic
        readings and are unusable; only its end-to-end numbers agree
        (within 2.4\% at 128\,k, 0.1\% elsewhere).
  \item \textbf{Every figure and table} --- regenerated by
        \path{scripts/lcfm_figures.py} from the CSVs above, written to
        \path{results/lcfm/figs/} and \path{results/lcfm/tables/} and
        \emph{included} by this document rather than copied into it.
\end{itemize}
